stories.title: FBI warns attackers are using the ARTEX AI penetration testing framework in global attacks

writeup.what_happened: According to BleepingComputer, the FBI has warned that threat actors are using ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework, to automate attacks against organizations worldwide. BleepingComputer reports that the activity includes a recent supply-chain breach involving ConnectWise that led to compromised Microsoft 365 customer environments. The available reporting does not describe ARTEX's techniques, indicators of compromise, or how the ConnectWise breach gave access to Microsoft 365 tenants.
writeup.why_it_matters: Exploitation is confirmed in the wild, and the reported impact falls on Microsoft 365 tenants, which suggests that trusted third-party access paths such as managed service providers and remote management tooling are part of the threat. AI-driven automation can shorten the time between initial access and follow-on activity, so defenders have less time to catch misuse of delegated or partner access. Because no indicators or techniques have been published, defenders have to hunt on behavior rather than on signatures.
recommended_actions: Review all third-party and MSP access to your Microsoft 365 tenant, including delegated admin relationships, partner relationships, and multi-tenant app consents, and remove anything that is not needed.
If you use ConnectWise products or a ConnectWise-based MSP, contact the vendor or provider to confirm whether you are affected, and rotate any credentials or secrets they hold.
Audit recent OAuth app consents, new service principal credentials, and permission grants in Entra ID, and investigate any you cannot explain.
Hunt for new or changed mailbox inbox rules and for sign-ins from unfamiliar infrastructure on admin and service accounts.
Watch for the FBI advisory to be published and add its indicators and techniques to your detections once they are available.

sources.title: FBI warns ARTEX AI hacking tool is powering global cyberattacks

hunting_steps: List all delegated admin, partner, and third-party app access to the tenant, and confirm each one with its business owner.
Review Entra ID audit activity from the last 30 days for application consents, new service principal credentials, and new permission grants.
Look for creation or modification of mailbox inbox rules, focusing on rules that forward, delete, or hide messages.
On endpoints managed through ConnectWise tooling, check for remote access agents launching shells or script interpreters.
Correlate any findings with sign-in logs to find unfamiliar IP addresses or countries for the same accounts.
Once the FBI publishes indicators for ARTEX, run them against these same data sources.

hunting_queries.title: OAuth consents and service principal credential changes
hunting_queries.kql: CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType in ("Consent to application.", "Add service principal credentials.", "Add delegated permission grant.", "Add app role assignment to service principal.") | project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, RawEventData | order by Timestamp desc

hunting_queries.title: New or modified mailbox inbox rules
hunting_queries.kql: CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules") | project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, RawEventData | order by Timestamp desc

hunting_queries.title: ConnectWise ScreenConnect agents spawning shells or script hosts
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe", "ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe") | where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "rundll32.exe", "mshta.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc

stories.title: TSMC confirms leak of employee personal data after threat actor auctions 6.9GB

writeup.what_happened: According to BleepingComputer, TSMC has confirmed that personal data belonging to its employees was leaked online. A threat actor had put up for auction 6.9GB of data it said was stolen from the company. BleepingComputer's headline connects the breach to a cloud provider, but the available reporting does not name the provider, the initial access method, or how many employees are affected.
writeup.why_it_matters: No vulnerability, product or attack technique has been disclosed, so there is no exposure to check in your own Windows, M365 or edge environments. The main downstream risk is phishing and social engineering aimed at TSMC staff, and at partners and suppliers whose contacts may appear in the leaked data. The breach also shows that third-party cloud providers holding HR or employee data are a weak point worth reviewing.
recommended_actions: If your organization works with TSMC, warn staff who deal with TSMC contacts that impersonation and phishing using leaked employee details is likely.
Review which third-party cloud and SaaS providers hold your own employee or HR data, and confirm their breach notification obligations and access controls.
Watch for follow-up disclosures from TSMC or the cloud provider about the intrusion vector before acting on any technical indicators.

sources.title: TSMC employee data breach linked to cloud provider

stories.title: DrayTek Vigor2960 path traversal and command injection flaws disclosed, fixed in 1.5.1.7

writeup.what_happened: NVD has published two high-severity flaws in the DrayTek Vigor2960 router, both in the web management CGI handler mainfunction.cgi. CVE-2026-129451 (CVSS 8.6) is a path traversal in the guest export function's filename parameter and affects versions up to 1.5.1.6. CVE-2026-129452 (CVSS 8.5) is a command injection through the jsondata parameter of the set_table function in 1.5.1.6. Both can be triggered remotely, and NVD lists 1.5.1.7 as the fix. NVD says exploit details are public, but other vulnerability data does not show confirmed public proof-of-concept code, so the sources disagree on this point.
writeup.why_it_matters: If a Vigor2960 management interface can be reached, an attacker could read files from the device or run commands on it, which would let them take over a perimeter router that sits in front of your Windows and M365 users. Neither CVE is in CISA KEV and the EPSS scores are low (0.5% and 2.2%). Still, DrayTek edge devices have been mass-exploited before, and NVD reports public exploit details, so exposed units should be patched quickly. DrayTek has also said another release with further fixes is planned, which means 1.5.1.7 may not be the last update needed.
recommended_actions: Find every DrayTek Vigor2960 in your estate and upgrade it to firmware 1.5.1.7 or later, then watch for DrayTek's next announced security release.
Block internet access to the Vigor2960 web management interface and limit administration to a dedicated management network or VPN.
Review router web and system logs for requests to mainfunction.cgi from unexpected sources, especially ones that reference guest export or table-setting functions.

If a device was exposed and unpatched, treat it as possibly compromised: check its configuration for unknown admin accounts, changed VPN or DNS settings, and new port forwards, and rotate the admin and VPN credentials it stores.
Check internal hosts for unusual traffic from the router's management IP, which could indicate an attacker moving inward from the device.

hunting_steps: List all DrayTek Vigor2960 devices using asset inventory and Defender for Endpoint device discovery, and record each one's firmware version.
Check which of those devices expose their web management interface to the internet, using external attack surface data or a firewall rule review.
Query Defender vulnerability management for the two CVE IDs to find flagged devices.
On exposed or unpatched devices, pull the router logs and look for requests to mainfunction.cgi from external addresses, as well as unexpected configuration changes.
Investigate any internal connections that start from the router's management IP to endpoints or servers.

hunting_queries.title: Devices flagged for the DrayTek Vigor2960 CVEs
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities | where CveId in ("CVE-2026-129451", "CVE-2026-129452") | project DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel

hunting_queries.title: Discovered DrayTek network devices and their models
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where Vendor has "DrayTek" or Model has "Vigor" | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Vendor, Model, DeviceType, OSVersion, PublicIP

stories.title: D-Link DIR-850L router firmware ships hard-coded console credentials (CVE-2026-129445)

writeup.what_happened: NVD published CVE-2026-129445 on 15 November 2026, describing hard-coded credentials in the console login component (the consolepwd binary) of D-Link DIR-850L firmware FW1.20WWb03. NVD rates it CVSS 8.4 (High) and says exploitation requires local access. The NVD entry states that an exploit has been released publicly, but other tracking data does not confirm that public proof-of-concept code exists, so the sources disagree on this point. No vendor advisory or fixed firmware is cited.
writeup.why_it_matters: The DIR-850L is a consumer and small-office router, so it is unlikely to be in managed enterprise estates. It may still appear in branch offices or on home networks used by remote workers. The flaw needs local access, is not in CISA KEV, and has a low EPSS of about 0.13%, so urgency is low. Hard-coded credentials cannot be rotated by the owner, though, so any reachable console on an affected device should be treated as open.
recommended_actions: Inventory DIR-850L routers on corporate, branch and sanctioned remote-work networks, and check which firmware they run.
Check D-Link's support channels for a firmware update or an end-of-life notice for the DIR-850L. If no fix exists, plan to replace affected units.
Until devices are replaced, restrict physical and local-network access to the router's console and management interfaces.
Treat any affected router on a network that carries corporate traffic as untrusted, and require VPN with device compliance checks for remote users behind such hardware.

hunting_steps: Use Defender for Endpoint device discovery to list network devices whose vendor is D-Link, and filter for the DIR-850L model.
For each device found, confirm the firmware version through its management interface or asset records, and note whether it runs FW1.20WWb03.
Check whether managed endpoints use a D-Link device as their default gateway on branch or home networks, and flag those users for hardware review.
Record affected devices and track them through replacement or firmware update.

hunting_queries.title: Discovered D-Link network devices (look for DIR-850L)
hunting_queries.kql:
DeviceInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Vendor has "D-Link" or Model has "DIR-850"
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, DeviceType, Vendor, Model, OSVersion, PublicIP

hunting_queries.title: TVM findings for CVE-2026-129445
hunting_queries.kql:
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-129445"
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel

stories.title: Cyrus SASL through 2.1.28: SRP mechanism flaw lets unauthenticated clients log in as any user

writeup.what_happened: NVD published CVE-2026-129483 (CVSS 9.3) on 15 November 2026. It describes an authentication bypass in the SRP server mechanism of Cyrus SASL through 2.1.28. The server-side SRP step does not validate the client's public value properly, so an unauthenticated network client can force a predictable shared secret. That lets the client authenticate as any existing user without the password and learn the session keys. NVD does not list affected vendor products or a fixed release.
writeup.why_it_matters: Cyrus SASL is embedded in many Linux mail, directory and IMAP services, and a successful bypass gives full account impersonation on whatever service uses it. Only deployments that offer the SRP mechanism should be exposed, so whether SRP is enabled decides real risk. There is no known exploitation, no public proof of concept, no KEV listing and an EPSS of 0.38%, so this is a prompt-patch and configuration review item rather than an emergency.
recommended_actions: Inventory Linux servers carrying Cyrus SASL (cyrus-sasl, libsasl2 packages), with internet-facing mail, LDAP and IMAP servers first.
Check whether the SRP mechanism plugin is installed and offered by each service. Where it is, remove the SRP plugin package or restrict the service's SASL mechanism list to exclude SRP.
Watch distribution and upstream Cyrus SASL advisories for a fixed release and apply it once available. The sources do not state a fixed version.

Review authentication logs of SASL-using services for successful SRP logins, especially from unexpected sources or for privileged accounts, and rotate credentials and session secrets if any look suspicious.

hunting_steps: Use Defender Vulnerability Management to list devices flagged for CVE-2026-129483 and devices with Cyrus SASL or libsasl2 version 2.1.28 or earlier installed.
On those hosts, check for an installed SRP plugin and whether SASL configuration files enable it in the mechanism list.
Identify which of those hosts expose SASL-authenticating services (SMTP submission, IMAP, LDAP) to untrusted networks by looking at inbound connections on the relevant ports.
Review the service logs on exposed hosts for SRP mechanism authentications and correlate them with source IPs and account activity.

hunting_queries.title: Devices flagged for CVE-2026-129483
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities | where CveId == "CVE-2026-129483" | project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel

hunting_queries.title: Cyrus SASL / libsasl2 software inventory on Linux
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | where SoftwareName has_any ("cyrus-sasl", "libsasl2", "cyrus_sasl", "sasl2") | project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion | order by DeviceName asc

hunting_queries.title: Inbound connections to SASL-using mail and directory ports on Linux
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted" | where LocalPort in (25, 143, 389, 465, 587, 636, 993) | join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where OSPlatform == "Linux" | distinct DeviceId) on DeviceId | summarize Connections = count(), RemoteIPs = dcount(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, LocalPort | order by Connections desc

explainer.concept: Missing public-value validation in SRP: the zero-key authentication bypass
explainer.dek: SRP is a password-authenticated key exchange in which a server that does not reject a malicious client public value can be forced to compute a predictable session key, letting an attacker log in without the password.
explainer.why_today: The critical Cyrus SASL flaw disclosed today is a failure of exactly this check in the SRP server mechanism. It is worth understanding because the same mistake recurs across key-exchange code, and Cyrus SASL sits underneath mail, directory and other Unix services.

parts.heading: How SRP is supposed to work
paragraphs: The Secure Remote Password protocol (SRP, specified in RFC 2945 and, for TLS, RFC 5054) lets a client prove it knows a password without sending it. The server stores a salt and a verifier derived from the password, not the password itself. During login, the client sends a public value A, the server sends a public value B, and both sides independently compute the same shared secret S. That secret yields a session key, and each side then sends a proof showing it derived the same key.

The design depends on the attacker being unable to compute S without the password. The server's version of S is built by multiplying A by a term derived from the stored verifier and raising the result to the server's private exponent, all modulo a large prime N. If A behaves like a normal random value, an attacker who lacks the password cannot predict S.

parts.heading: Where the check goes missing
paragraphs: The SRP-6a specification requires the server to abort if A modulo N equals zero. The reason is arithmetic: if A is zero, or N, or any multiple of N, the server's computation collapses to zero no matter what the password, verifier or server secret is. The attacker then knows the shared secret is zero, derives the session key, and builds a valid client proof without ever knowing the password.

Today's NVD description of the Cyrus SASL issue matches this class: the server-side SRP step does not properly validate the client's public value, so an unauthenticated client can force a predictable shared secret, authenticate as any existing user and learn the session keys. The same family of bugs appears elsewhere as small-subgroup and invalid-curve attacks on Diffie-Hellman and elliptic-curve key exchange, where an unchecked peer value pins the result to a small, guessable set.

parts.heading: Exposure and what it looks like in logs
paragraphs: Cyrus SASL is a pluggable authentication library used by software such as mail servers, LDAP directories and IMAP servers, and it is also embedded in appliances. SRP is one optional mechanism among many; whether it is compiled, packaged and offered depends on the distribution, the product and its configuration, so exposure is not uniform and must be checked per system. A service that does not offer SRP in its mechanism list is not reachable through this path.

Successful exploitation looks like a normal successful login, because the protocol completes correctly from the server's point of view. The signals to look for are SRP-mechanism authentications at all, especially if your clients never use SRP, successful logins for privileged or service accounts from unfamiliar sources, and logins with no preceding failures for accounts that would normally use a different mechanism.

takeaways: Inventory Linux and Unix servers and appliances that link Cyrus SASL (mail transfer agents, IMAP servers, OpenLDAP and similar) and record the installed version against the affected range of 2.1.28 and earlier.

On each service, list the advertised SASL mechanisms and remove SRP from the allowed mechanism list wherever it is not explicitly required, which closes this path even before a fixed release is available.
Ask vendors of mail gateways, directory appliances and other edge products whether they bundle Cyrus SASL with the SRP plugin, since NVD does not yet list affected products.
Forward SASL authentication logs to Sentinel and alert on any SRP-mechanism authentication, prioritising successful logins for administrative and service accounts.

When reviewing any key-exchange or PAKE code your organisation owns or buys, confirm that peer public values are validated (non-zero modulo N for SRP, subgroup and curve checks for Diffie-Hellman and ECDH).

good_news.headline: YARA-X 1.23.0 released with 4 improvements and 16 bug fixes
good_news.summary: SANS Internet Storm Center reports that version 1.23.0 of YARA-X, the rewrite of the YARA pattern-matching engine used for malware detection and hunting, has been released. According to SANS ISC handler Didier Stevens, the release brings 4 improvements and 16 bug fixes.
